newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ watchdog won't intervene in INL's Sky TV buy-in.
newsitem.headline: NZ watchdog won't intervene in INL's Sky TV buy-in.

text.p: The anti-monopolies New Zealand Commerce Commission said on Friday it would not, on current information available to it, intervene in plans by News Corp's Independent Newspapers Ltd to buy into New Zealand pay television company Sky Network TV.

"It (the commission) has no plans to intervene in the proposal that INL and associated companies acquire a majority shareholding in Sky Network Television Ltd," commission chairman Alan Bollard said in a statement.
Last month INL said it was in talks to buy a substantial holding in New Zealand's largest pay-TV operator.
"We have investigated the proposal and decided that unless it changes substantially we will take no action against it," Bollard said.

The Commerce Act prohibits business acquisitions which result in dominance being acquired or strenthened in any market. Bollard said INL, 49.5 percent owned by Murdoch's News, had not applied for approval and the commission's decision did not give the legal protection that could come from a clearance or authorisation.
He said other parties could challenge the acquisition if they wished.
Bollard said the commission gave particular consideration to links the proposal would create between Sky Network and News.

Murdoch controls BSkyB and other satellite pay-TV companies in the United States, Japan, Latin America and Australia, and analysts believe a New Zealand Sky purchase would be another link in a global satellite pay-TV network.
Despite its name, Sky Network is not connected to BSkyB.
Sky Network is currently half-owned by U.S.-based HKP Partnership, a group of powerful U.S. companies including Bell Atlantic , Ameritech, Time Warner and Tele-Communications Inc.
Bollard noted that News owned the rights to televise various sports events including New Zealand rugby.

"The commission concluded that the links would not prevent other television broadcasters from obtaining competing programmes and the television broadcasting market in New Zealand would remain competitive," Bollard said.
"The commission maintained its previous views that free-to-air and pay television operate in the same market, and that print media are in a separate market."
He noted that Friday's decision related only to INL's plan to buy into Sky and the involvement of any other party would be dealt with separately.
